_comment: Per-row ceilings on the alpine/official ratio, enforced by
assert-perf-budgets.py. These are REGRESSION ALARMS, not parity targets:
the goal is <= 1.00, the budget is where a build has gone visibly wrong.
A budget is set from the 99th percentile of what a SINGLE probe shot reads,
because that is what this gate sees: the inline probe runs each browser
once per target and divides. It is NOT set from the median ratio. Sizing a
budget off the median produces a gate that fails on healthy builds.
Seeded from 90 paired shots: perf-probe runs 34289013835 / 34289022039 /
34289030252, three browsers x n=10, drawn across four runner CPU models
(EPYC 7763, EPYC 9V74, Xeon 6973P-C, Xeon 8370C). Ratios are only
comparable within one job, so each shot is paired to its own same-runner
control.
Two populations, and the difference matters when reading a green run:
TIGHT ROWS - dispersion under ~10%, so the budget tracks real
performance and a breach is a real regression. locator_click, int_math,
libm_fmod, and every webkit row except eval_rtt/click_force. int_math read
5-9x when chromium shipped with DCHECKs on; this is the sharpest detector
we have.
DISPERSION-BOUND ROWS - single-shot spread exceeds the signal, so the
ceiling is set by noise and only catches a catastrophe. firefox launch
(median 0.97, p99 2.01), firefox js_alloc (median 1.20, p99 2.18),
chromium screenshot (median 1.00-1.26 by CPU, p99 1.82). Do NOT read
these budgets as an allowance: firefox launch is AT parity and its 2.15
ceiling is measurement noise, not a target. Repeats barely help - n=5
only moves firefox launch's p99 from 2.01 to 1.72, at five times the
probe cost - so the gate stays at n=1 and these rows stay loose.
Two rows are CPU-model-dependent rather than noisy, which is why their
budgets look wide: chromium layout reads 1.27 on EPYC 9V74 against
1.59-1.62 on EPYC 7763, and chromium screenshot inverts it, 1.26 on 9V74
against 1.00 on 7763. Both are reproducible across replicate jobs.
A row whose budget must be raised is a finding. Raise it in the same PR that
causes it, so the number moves where a reviewer can see it.
